uap-archive-aaro-atmospheric-wakes-case.title: Atmospheric Wakes
uap-archive-aaro-atmospheric-wakes-case.summary: Three infrared videos over the Middle East and Mediterranean appeared to show an anomalous propulsion signature.

uap-archive-aaro-eglin-uap-case.title: Eglin UAP
uap-archive-aaro-eglin-uap-case.summary: A pilot near Eglin AFB reported an object at about 16,000 ft on radar and electro-optical/infrared.

uap-archive-aaro-southeast-asia-triangle.title: Southeast Asia Triangles
uap-archive-aaro-southeast-asia-triangle.summary: Satellite imagery showed six triangular objects in formation, flagged as potentially anomalous.

uap-archive-aaro-western-united-states-c.title: Western United States
uap-archive-aaro-western-united-states-c.summary: A 2021 report of five equidistant infrared lights at 20,000–40,000 ft, flagged as a possible airspace incursion.

uap-archive-jal-1628-1986.title: Japan Airlines Flight 1628 UFO Records, 1986
uap-archive-jal-1628-1986.summary: FAA records on the 1986 Japan Airlines Flight 1628 UFO sighting over Alaska.

uap-archive-navy-flir1-2004.title: FLIR1
uap-archive-navy-flir1-2004.summary: An infrared video recorded on 14 November 2004 by a U.S. Navy aircraft during USS Nimitz carrier strike group operations off Southern California; the object was later nicknamed the “Tic Tac”.

uap-archive-navy-gimbal-2015.title: Gimbal
uap-archive-navy-gimbal-2015.summary: An infrared video recorded in 2015 by a U.S. Navy aircraft from the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group operating off the U.S. East Coast.

uap-archive-northeastern-orb-sightings.title: Northeastern Orb Sighting
uap-archive-northeastern-orb-sightings.summary: FBI orb videos and FD-302/FD-1057 reports from the Northeastern United States (2021–2026).

disclosure-six-spheres-2025.title: Six Points Without a Place
disclosure-six-spheres-2025.summary: On 29 July 2025 at 20:22Z the crew of a 65th Special Operations Squadron aircraft, on its way to its tasking, reported “6X SMALL SPHERICAL OBJECTS GROUPED TOGETHER” that “SEEMED TO BE AGILE, FREQUENTLY CHNAGING DIRECTION”, at an estimated flight level 220 and an estimated “48OMPH”. Nothing measured the objects, and every position in the report is blacked out, so the case has no place. The one-minute infrared recording released with the report shows a group of small bright points: first crossing past a lattice tower in a straight line, then for half a minute against a blank background, where the group spreads, splits into two threes and closes again. That rearrangement is the one thing the recording lets us measure; without a range it is not known whether it spans metres or kilometres.

disclosure-virginia-2024.title: The Active Virginia Coast Case
disclosure-virginia-2024.summary: The US Navy reported approximately 100 aerial objects and two probably unmanned surface systems in an area off the Virginia coast. AARO listed the case as remaining under active analysis.

disclosure-east-coast-drones-2024.title: The East Coast Drone Flap
disclosure-east-coast-drones-2024.summary: From mid-November 2024, nightly reports of large drones over New Jersey and neighbouring states produced weeks of national coverage, emergency briefings and temporary flight restrictions. Four federal agencies assessed more than 5,000 tips and identified nothing anomalous.

disclosure-eastern-mediterranean-2024.title: The Diamond Seen Only in Short-Wave Infrared
disclosure-eastern-mediterranean-2024.summary: On 25 January 2024 an aircraft of the 33rd Special Operations Squadron, in transit over the eastern Mediterranean, watched an object for about two minutes, 05:09–05:11Z. Its mission report describes a “ROUND DIAMOND SHAPE WITH STRAIGHT, NON MANUEVERABLE "TAIL"” flying at “APPROX 434 KNOTS” that “ONLY APPEARED ON THE SWIR CAMERA”, the short-wave infrared. A recording of 1 min 6 s from the same mission, released separately, shows a bright body with a fainter upright element below it, visible in one camera and lost when the operator switches to visible light. The report records no range to the object, its grid references are blacked out down to the easting, and its own first and last coordinates do not fit the speed it gives.

disclosure-north-aegean-2023.title: Turns above the North Aegean
disclosure-north-aegean-2023.summary: On 27 October 2023 at 00:35Z the crew of a 33rd Special Operations Squadron aircraft, on its way from Larissa to its tasking, reported a “UAP FLYING JUST ABOVE THE SURFACE OF THE OCEAN WATER” over the north Aegean that “TOOK MULTIPLE 90 DEGREE TURNS AT AN ESTIMATED 80 MPH”, and lost it from the picture at 00:38Z. The infrared recording released with the report, 2 min 57 s long, shows a small bright point that crosses the view and changes direction sharply while the sea behind it stays put in the frame, and then sits for 82 seconds in a tracking reticle until it fades. Neither the report nor the recording gives a range or a field of view, so the point's size and the 80 mph cannot be tested. Two days later the same squadron reported an object of the same description flying straight towards Crete; its 24-second recording shows a point moving in a straight line against the clouds.

disclosure-western-us-2023.title: The Western U.S. Event
disclosure-western-us-2023.summary: In October 2023, federal law enforcement special agents surveying for illegal drone launches near a sensitive national security site in the western United States reported orange orbs releasing clusters of smaller red orbs, objects that mimicked road vehicles, and kite-shaped objects at close range. AARO attributes roughly 60 percent of the activity to military countermeasure flares and states that roughly 40 percent remains unresolved. No radar return, photograph or film of the phenomena has been released.

disclosure-test-site-2023.title: Bronze, Gray, or Just a Light
disclosure-test-site-2023.summary: In September 2023, according to three FBI interviews taken that month, five people in three vehicles were driving through a gate on their way to a test site when an object was seen in a clear sky for five to ten seconds before it vanished. One account describes a “cigar shaped object”, “metallic bronze in color”; another a “linear object”, “metallic / gray in color”; the third only “a bright light over the horizon” and the thought that it “might have been a meteor”. One interview records that no photos or video were taken. The day and every place name are blacked out, and the release holds no analysis. A sketch published with the interviews is dated, by its file name alone, seven months later, and none of the interviews mentions it.

disclosure-balloon-2023.title: The 2023 Balloon and the Shootdowns
disclosure-balloon-2023.summary: A Chinese high-altitude balloon crossed North America and was shot down off South Carolina. In the following week, after air defence radar filters were adjusted, three further unidentified objects were engaged and destroyed over Alaska, Yukon and Lake Huron — none of which was ever conclusively identified.

uap-archive-western-us-event.title: Western US Event
uap-archive-western-us-event.summary: Documents and imagery released under the Department of War's PURSUE program for the “Western US Event”.

disclosure-iraq-2022.title: The Same Paragraph Twice over Iraq
disclosure-iraq-2022.summary: On 5 May 2022 two crews of different squadrons over northern Iraq filed mission reports that describe small objects in the same paragraph, word for word down to the misspelling “SPORATICALLY”: “UAPs” moving “AT VARIOUS SPEEDS BETWEEN 80-180 MPH”, at an altitude the crew was “UNABLE TO DETERMINE”, “APPROXIMATELY 1-2 METERS” in size, which “DID NOT HINDER THE MISSION”. The 20th Attack Squadron watched them from 05:24Z to 07:04Z, in daylight and in a dust storm; the 196th logged them at 20:26Z, at night, and described what it saw as “UAS”. The two recordings released with the reports show small dark dots over hazy ground in infrared and in colour by day, so they belong to the morning report. Neither report says how the speed was measured or how far away the objects were, so neither the speed nor the size can be tested.

disclosure-colorado-springs-2022.title: The Object over Cheyenne Mountain
disclosure-colorado-springs-2022.summary: In February 2022 five U.S. Army soldiers from one unit saw a white object hold still over Cheyenne Mountain, Colorado, and then vanish. The file holds two FBI interviews taken two and three years later and an undated analysis that attributes the sighting, with low confidence, to sunlight reflected off snow onto low cloud. No photograph was taken, the five drawings and the FBI artist's sketch are not in the file, and the accounts disagree on the time of day, the duration and what the object looked like.

uap-archive-colorado-springs-2022.title: Colorado Springs UAP Incident
uap-archive-colorado-springs-2022.summary: FBI unresolved-UAP reports and an ICA analysis on a 2022 incident near Colorado Springs.

disclosure-persian-gulf-2020.title: Ten Sightings over the Gulf
disclosure-persian-gulf-2020.summary: Between 16 July and 2 November 2020 the 482nd Attack Squadron, flying intelligence missions over the Persian Gulf from Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait, logged ten sightings of unidentified objects in six mission reports and one debrief form. For most of them the reports give a time, a partly blacked-out grid reference and the word “UAP”, and nothing else: no size, shape, colour or speed, and no assessment. Four recordings released separately carry the dates of two of the sightings in titles given by whoever uploaded them; the office that released them says such material lacks a substantiated chain of custody.

disclosure-colorado-drones-2019.title: The Colorado Drone Swarms
disclosure-colorado-drones-2019.summary: For several weeks, large unmanned aircraft were reported flying nightly grid patterns over rural Colorado and Nebraska. Sheriffs, the FAA, the FBI and a state task force investigated. No operator was ever identified and no enforcement action followed.

disclosure-san-diego-drones-2019.title: Off San Diego, July 2019: the Ships' Logs
disclosure-san-diego-drones-2019.summary: In July 2019 the logs and reports of US Navy ships off San Diego recorded drones around them. The CIC log of USS Rafael Peralta has on 15 July at 20:57 “DRONE 1 SPOTTED”, then “BRIDGE VISUALLY SITED [sic] AN EXCESS OF 4 DRONES”, and on 16 July at 01:33 “BRIDGE HOLDS 6 DRONES OFF OF STBD BOW”. A brief of USS Paul Hamilton of 17 July is titled “Interaction with UAS”, and the Navy’s incident database records four drones around the same ship in an incident dated 29 July, three of them “identified visually as quadcopters”. The documents call the objects drones and UAS; none says who flew them: “Point of origin of all UASs is unknown.”

etna-2018.title: Mt. Etna infrared video
etna-2018.summary: A military infrared sensor recorded an object near Mt. Etna in 2018. AARO later published an analysis of optical effects near the hot volcanic plume.

al-taqaddum-2017.title: Al Taqaddum infrared footage
al-taqaddum-2017.summary: In October 2017 an infrared sensor aboard a military aerostat filmed an object above Al Taqaddum. AARO's published assessment found a cluster of balloons was consistent with the footage.

disclosure-mosul-orb-2016.title: The Mosul Orb
disclosure-mosul-orb-2016.summary: A short clip from a US reconnaissance platform showing a small spherical object crossing the field of view over Mosul. AARO presented it publicly as an example of an unresolved case.

gimbal-2015.title: GIMBAL Navy video
gimbal-2015.summary: GIMBAL is one of the January 2015 Navy clips officially released by the Pentagon in April 2020. The video is authenticated, but interpretations of what it depicts are separate claims.

gofast-2015.title: GOFAST Navy video
gofast-2015.summary: GOFAST is another January 2015 Navy recording officially released by the Pentagon. The footage is genuine, but apparent speed and range require care with parallax; the clip alone does not settle the object's identity.

disclosure-roosevelt-2014.title: East Coast: the W-72 Reports
disclosure-roosevelt-2014.summary: Between June 2013 and April 2014 three Navy F/A-18 squadrons flying from NAS Oceana filed seven hazard reports from warning area W-72 off Virginia; the Navy’s FOIA reading room holds them as printed on 29 May 2019. On the night of 23 April 2014 a VFA-11 crew found two radar tracks at “0.0 Mach” and 15,000 and 12,000 feet, used “multiple on-board sensors to verify that HUAD1 and HUAD2 were small IR significant objects and not false radar track files”, and saw two more objects cross the infrared field of view “at a high speed”. The next day two VFA-11 jets held a stable radar track at 11,000 feet but could not see anything. Other crews saw a white aircraft with “an approximately 5 foot wingspan”, a silver object “approximately the size of a suitcase”, and a white object “approximately the size and shape of a drone or missile” that passed about 200 feet away. The reports spell out HUAD as “Hazard Unidentified Aerial Device”, give as the cause objects operating “without coordination”, and name no operator. In 2023 Ryan Graves, a VFA-11 pilot in 2014, told Congress under oath that the detections began “After upgrades were made to our jet’s radar systems”.

puerto-rico-2013.title: Puerto Rico infrared footage
puerto-rico-2013.summary: In 2013 a U.S. border patrol aircraft recorded two objects near Aguadilla. AARO analyzed the footage and assessed sky lanterns as a plausible explanation.

disclosure-aguadilla-2013.title: Aguadilla
disclosure-aguadilla-2013.summary: Infrared footage from a border patrol aircraft shows an object flying over terrain, entering the ocean, emerging, and splitting in two. For years it was presented as the best evidence for objects moving between media.

disclosure-ladakh-2012.title: Ladakh
disclosure-ladakh-2012.summary: Army and border police units in Ladakh logged several hundred sightings of luminous objects over six months, initially suspected to be Chinese surveillance drones. A scientific team was sent to investigate.

disclosure-hangzhou-2010.title: Hangzhou Airport
disclosure-hangzhou-2010.summary: Xiaoshan International Airport suspended operations for roughly an hour after an unidentified object was reported in its airspace. Flights were diverted and delayed. Chinese authorities later indicated a military connection but released no detail.

disclosure-harare-2008.title: The Harare Alert
disclosure-harare-2008.summary: A CIA information report sent on 3 July 2008 to forty-seven named addressees says that on the afternoon of 2 July an unidentified object hovered over Harare International Airport and was observed, “possibly by both radar and optical means”. Observers on the ground described a disc with a hollow centre and rotating lights that changed colour before it climbed quickly out of sight. People who knew of the incident debated whether it was a foreign reconnaissance device or of extraterrestrial origin. According to the report, the incident led to a decision to place a Zimbabwean unit, whose name is blacked out, on high alert. The report is marked not finally evaluated, and about two thirds of it is blacked out.

disclosure-stephenville-2008.title: Stephenville
disclosure-stephenville-2008.summary: After a wave of reports of a large, silent object with lights, independent researchers obtained FAA radar data under FOIA, which showed an unidentified track in the area together with F-16 activity the air base had previously denied.

disclosure-ohare-2006.title: O'Hare
disclosure-ohare-2006.summary: A dozen airport employees reported a grey disc-shaped object hovering over Gate C17, which then departed vertically at speed, said to leave a hole in the cloud layer.

nimitz-2004.title: FLIR1 / Nimitz footage
nimitz-2004.summary: The US Department of Defense authenticated Navy footage from November 2004 and officially released it in 2020. Authentication establishes the footage's origin, not an extraterrestrial explanation.

disclosure-mexico-2004.title: The Mexican Air Force FLIR
disclosure-mexico-2004.summary: A Mexican Air Force surveillance aircraft on an anti-narcotics patrol recorded eleven objects on infrared that appeared to surround it. The Defence Ministry released the footage publicly. Analysis subsequently matched the objects to burning gas flares at the Cantarell offshore oil field.

phoenix-1997.title: Phoenix Lights
phoenix-1997.summary: On March 13, 1997, NUFORC logged multiple calls from Arizona residents reporting lights, often in a V-shaped formation. Witness descriptions vary; the reports do not establish what caused every observation.

disclosure-varginha-1996.title: Varginha
disclosure-varginha-1996.summary: Three young women reported seeing an unusual creature in the town. An elaborate narrative grew around the account, involving a military capture operation, transport to a hospital, and the death of the captured being.

disclosure-bariloche-1995.title: The Bariloche Approach
disclosure-bariloche-1995.summary: On a night approach into Bariloche, the crew of a scheduled Boeing 727 reported a light that paced the aircraft, stopped, climbed vertically and repositioned ahead of them. The approach was held because the town and the airport had lost power. A second crew, the tower and people on the ground reported the same light.

disclosure-ariel-school-1994.title: Ariel School
disclosure-ariel-school-1994.summary: During a break, a group of children reported an object landing and the presence of beings at the edge of the school grounds. Interviews were conducted within days and partly recorded, including by a Harvard psychiatrist’s team.

disclosure-cosford-1993.title: The Cosford Incident
disclosure-cosford-1993.summary: Over one night, RAF personnel at two bases, police and dozens of civilians reported a large triangular craft and a beam of light sweeping the ground. The MOD’s UFO desk escalated the case internally as one of the most significant it had handled.

disclosure-calvine-1990.title: Calvine
disclosure-calvine-1990.summary: Two young men took six photographs of a large, static diamond-shaped object, near which a military aircraft passed. The negatives were passed to the Ministry of Defence and lost; a single copy surfaced only in 2022.

disclosure-belgian-wave-1990.title: The Belgian Wave
disclosure-belgian-wave-1990.summary: According to a summary by The National Archives (UK), on 30–31 March 1990 ‘large, unknown triangular-shaped objects were reported’ over Belgium after months of sightings; radar ‘reportedly tracked an unknown object over central Belgium’, the Belgian Air Force scrambled two F-16s, and ‘The pilots reported no sightings, and the object was not identified.’ A newspaper article of 2000, filed in the release, says the F-16s were ‘armed with missiles’.

disclosure-voronezh-1989.title: Voronezh
disclosure-voronezh-1989.summary: The TASS agency issued a dispatch reporting the landing of an object and the emergence of a being from it. The report circulated worldwide as the first such statement from an official Soviet agency.

disclosure-jal1628-1986.title: JAL 1628
disclosure-jal1628-1986.summary: On the evening of 17 November 1986 the crew of Japan Air Lines flight 1628, a Boeing 747 freighter bound from Iceland to Anchorage, reported lights near their aircraft over interior Alaska; the captain later wrote of “two spaceships and a Mother ship”. Controllers at the FAA’s Anchorage Center and at the military control centre at Elmendorf saw intermittent radar returns where the pilot reported traffic. The FAA released its file in March 1987: its Technical Center found that the second radar target was “a split radar return from the JAL Boeing 747”, the recorded radar data showed no other target, and the agency said it had not tried to determine what the crew saw. The file, 41 units in the National Archives, is public.

jal-1628-1986.title: Japan Airlines Flight 1628
jal-1628-1986.summary: The crew of Japan Airlines cargo flight 1628 reported unusual lights over Alaska in November 1986. FAA records document the interviews and checks, but the agency said it could not confirm another aircraft or object.

disclosure-noite-ovnis-1986.title: Noite Oficial dos OVNIs
disclosure-noite-ovnis-1986.summary: Brazilian air defence radars detected multiple unidentified targets simultaneously. Mirage III and F-5E fighters were scrambled; some crews reported radar and visual contact. The Air Minister confirmed the event at a press conference.

disclosure-dalnegorsk-1986.title: Dalnegorsk
disclosure-dalnegorsk-1986.summary: Residents watched a reddish sphere fly over the town and strike a rocky hillside, where it reportedly burned for about an hour. Investigators from the Soviet Academy of Sciences collected metallic residue, glassy droplets and mesh-like fragments from the site.

disclosure-hessdalen-1984.title: Hessdalen
disclosure-hessdalen-1984.summary: Unknown lights began to show up in the Hessdalen valley in December 1981. With no state institution taking it up, five people set up Project Hessdalen, and from 21 January to 26 February 1984 its volunteers watched the valley with cameras and spectral gratings, a radar, a spectrum analyser, a magnetometer, a seismograph, a laser, Geiger counters and infrared viewers, helped by the Norwegian Defence Research Establishment and universities. Of 188 reports, 135 were put down to known lights; the radar made 36 recordings, three of them probably of a light that was also seen. The report, signed by Erling Strand on 5 January 1985, concludes: “We have not found out what this phenomenon is.”

disclosure-hudson-valley-1983.title: The Hudson Valley Wave
disclosure-hudson-valley-1983.summary: For several years thousands of people across the Hudson Valley reported a huge, silent, slow-moving boomerang of lights. A group of private pilots from a local airfield subsequently admitted flying formations of light aircraft with modified lighting, deliberately, on those nights.

disclosure-trans-en-provence-1981.title: Trans-en-Provence
disclosure-trans-en-provence-1981.summary: On 8 January 1981, at about 5 pm, a man working on a terrace behind his house in the Var saw a craft come down, rest on the ground for a few seconds and leave. Next morning he showed his wife the marks; neighbours alerted the gendarmerie, which photographed two concentric circles 2.20 and 2.40 m across and took samples. GEPAN, the group at the French space agency CNES that studied such reports, published the case in March 1983 as technical note no. 16. Its laboratories found the soil compacted and heated to no more than 600°, and Dr M. Bounias of INRA found pigment losses in wild alfalfa that were greater nearer the trace. GEPAN concluded that the interpretations were “trop diverses et vagues” (too varied and vague) to confirm the witness’s account, and that whether the plant changes matched his description “reste à savoir” (remains to be seen).

rendlesham-1980.title: Rendlesham Forest incident
rendlesham-1980.summary: In December 1980, US service personnel reported unusual lights near RAF Woodbridge. UK archival files document the correspondence, while interpretations of the eyewitness accounts remain disputed.

disclosure-arequipa-1980.title: Arequipa
disclosure-arequipa-1980.summary: Personnel at a Peruvian air base observed a stationary balloon-shaped object at dawn. A Su-22 was scrambled and, by the pilot’s account, fired a cannon burst that had no effect, after which the object climbed away from the pursuing aircraft.

disclosure-manises-1979.title: Manises
disclosure-manises-1979.summary: The captain of a scheduled flight diverted to Valencia after bright red lights approached his aircraft. The Spanish air force scrambled a Mirage F1, whose pilot also reported a sighting.

disclosure-kaikoura-1978.title: Kaikoura
disclosure-kaikoura-1978.summary: An Australian television crew filmed a series of bright lights from aboard an aircraft, correlated in time with returns on the Wellington radar. The footage circled the world as the first “UFO filmed from the cockpit”.

disclosure-valentich-1978.title: Frederick Valentich
disclosure-valentich-1978.summary: A 20-year-old pilot on a night flight over Bass Strait reported an object with four bright lights above and around his Cessna, said it was “not an aircraft”, and reported engine trouble. The transmission ended with an unidentified metallic sound. Neither he nor the aircraft was ever found.

disclosure-italy-1978.title: The Italian Wave of 1978
disclosure-italy-1978.summary: An intensified wave of reports led to an administrative decision: the Aeronautica Militare was formally tasked with collecting and investigating UAP reports. Italy has therefore had an unbroken state documentary record from 1978 to the present.

disclosure-petrozavodsk-1977.title: Petrozavodsk
disclosure-petrozavodsk-1977.summary: A vast luminous phenomenon described as a “jellyfish” shedding rays toward the ground appeared over the city. The event produced a wave of reports across Karelia and led to the creation of a Soviet research programme.

colares-1977.title: Operação Prato, Brazil
colares-1977.summary: In 1977–78 Brazilian military investigators collected testimony, photographs and sketches of lights in Pará. Surviving operation records include locations, times and descriptions.

tehran-1976.title: Tehran aerial observations
tehran-1976.summary: A declassified U.S. document recounts civilian calls and Iranian military aircraft observations in September 1976, including reports of a bright light and interrupted communications.

disclosure-lago-cote-1971.title: The Lago de Cote Photograph
disclosure-lago-cote-1971.summary: During a government aerial survey for a hydroelectric project, a cartographic camera firing automatically every 13 seconds recorded a sharp disc-shaped object over Lago de Cote. Nobody on board saw anything; the object was noticed in processing, and it appears on one frame and on neither neighbour.

disclosure-minot-afb-1968.title: Minot AFB
disclosure-minot-afb-1968.summary: In the early hours of 24 October 1968 airmen at missile sites around Minot AFB in North Dakota reported a bright light, and a B-52 flying practice approaches near the base had an unidentified return on its own radar. The crew photographed the scope, and while the return stayed with the aircraft its UHF transmitter would not work. Project Blue Book’s record card gives “Possible (PLASMA)” for the radar and for the sighting from the aircraft, and “Probable (AIRCRAFT)(B-52)” and “Probable Astro (SIRIUS)” for the sightings from the ground (NAID 302580672, image 1). The base’s report had listed among “FOUR OCCURANCES THAT CANNOT BE CORRELATED OR EXPLAINED AT THIS LEVEL” “WHAT CAUSED THE AIRCRAFT RADAR ECHO” and the “AIRCRAFT LOSS OF UHF TRANSMISSION” (image 15). The scope photographs are not in the file as published.

disclosure-himalaya-1968.title: The Crater at Baltichaur
disclosure-himalaya-1968.summary: A CIA information report distributed on 11 April 1968 lists seven sightings of bright objects between 19 February and 25 March 1968, over south Ladakh, north-east Nepal, north Sikkim, western Bhutan and the Kaski region of Nepal. The last entry adds, in one sentence, that a huge metallic disc-shaped object was found in a crater at Baltichaur, five miles north-east of Pokhara. The report is marked not finally evaluated, its source is blacked out, and it says nothing more about the object.

disclosure-shag-harbour-1967.title: Shag Harbour
disclosure-shag-harbour-1967.summary: Residents and RCMP officers watched an object descend into the water near shore. A Coast Guard search was launched on the assumption of an air crash. No missing aircraft was ever identified.

disclosure-cussac-1967.title: Cussac
disclosure-cussac-1967.summary: Two siblings reported a bright sphere and four small figures in a meadow. The gendarmerie investigated the same day, producing a protocol that later became part of the GEIPAN archive.

disclosure-falcon-lake-1967.title: Falcon Lake
disclosure-falcon-lake-1967.summary: Stefan Michalak, an industrial mechanic from Winnipeg, said that on 20 May 1967, while prospecting north of Falcon Beach, he saw two objects come down, that one landed, and that it burned him as it rose when he had touched it. He was treated for burns that night and his doctor recorded “first degree burns to the upper abdominal wall”; an RCMP constable who saw him that afternoon thought the marks on his chest “looked like marks that were caused by rubbing ash onto the skin”. No radioactivity was found on him or his clothes in May. In June Michalak and a partner brought soil, moss, a steel tape and remnants of his shirt from the site they had found; those samples were radioactive, and in July a federal radiation officer found a smear of radium-226 contamination no larger than 100 square inches in a crack of the rock there. In 1969 a scientist of the National Research Council judged it “highly probable” that crushed uranium ore produced all the radioactivity reported. The RCMP closed its file unable to resolve the burns, his illness and the circle on the rock.

disclosure-malmstrom-1967.title: Malmstrom AFB
disclosure-malmstrom-1967.summary: According to officer accounts, in March 1967 a series of Minuteman missiles went to a “no-go” state within a short interval, while security personnel simultaneously reported UAP sightings. This is the most frequently cited argument for UAP interest in nuclear weapons.

westall-1966.title: Westall witnesses
westall-1966.summary: On April 6, 1966, schoolchildren and teachers near Melbourne reported seeing an unusual object. ABC interviews preserve witness memories, not proof of any particular origin.

disclosure-exeter-1965.title: Exeter
disclosure-exeter-1965.summary: In the early hours of 3 September 1965 an 18-year-old hitchhiker on Route 150 south-west of Exeter, New Hampshire, saw “a group of five bright red lights” over a house and a field, watched them “for about 15 minutes” and went to the police station (NAID 302543878, image 97). Patrolman Eugene F. Bertrand Jr. drove him back; in the field “a group of five bright red lights came from behind a group of trees near us”, so close that Bertrand “fell to the ground and started to draw my gun” (image 99). Patrolman David R. Hunt, called by radio, saw the lights “about ½ mile over a field to the South East” at what he estimated as 100 feet (image 98). Neither the hitchhiker nor Bertrand could make out a form, and Bertrand heard “no sound or vibration” (image 99). The Air Force’s investigating officer found no probable cause (image 100), and Blue Book’s record card concludes “UNIDENTIFIED” (image 1).

disclosure-valensole-1965.title: Valensole
disclosure-valensole-1965.summary: A lavender farmer reported an ovoid object landed in his field with two small figures beside it. Gendarmes documented ground marks the same day. The affected patch of lavender reportedly failed to grow normally for years afterwards.

disclosure-socorro-1964.title: Socorro
disclosure-socorro-1964.summary: On 24 April 1964, at about 5:45 p.m., Officer Lonnie Zamora of the Socorro Police Department, New Mexico, broke off a chase to check on a roar and a flame south of the town. In the account he gave that night, an object stood off the road with two people beside it: “TWO PERSONS IN APPARENT WHITE COVERALLS”, as the FBI’s teletype put it the next day (Section 9, p. 226), who “appeared normal in shape--but possibly they were small adults or large kids” (Serial 438, p. 12). The object then rose with a roar and a flame and flew off. The state police sergeant and the undersheriff who answered his radio calls found four smouldering areas and four depressions; that evening Capt. R. T. Holder measured them while an FBI agent set rocks around them. Project Blue Book’s record card marks the case “Unknown” and comments: “Effort to date cannot place vehicle at site. Case carried as UNIDENTIFIED pending additional data.” (NAID 302532129, image 4)

disclosure-conde-1963.title: The Conde Sphere
disclosure-conde-1963.summary: On 8 November 1963 Radio Tupi in Rio de Janeiro reported that a large metal sphere with windows had fallen in the centre of Conde, in Bahia, gouging a hole four metres deep, with a human body inside. The Foreign Broadcast Information Service took the report down, and a note on its transcript dated 13 November records a request to the State Department to say whether the embassy had anything more. The embassy in Rio asked its consulate in Salvador. On 20 November it sent the Department an airgram titled “Negative Report on UFO”: the consul wrote that no one in the area had seen such an object and called the story “apparently fabricated in Rio”, and two Salvador papers had carried a denial by the Ministry of Aeronautics and a piece called “The Airship that wasn’t there”. The Department marked the airgram “NOTED - NO ACTION” and filed it.

disclosure-hill-1961.title: Betty and Barney Hill
disclosure-hill-1961.summary: On the night of 19/20 September 1961, “between 20/0001 and 20/0100”, a couple driving south on Route 3 near Lincoln, New Hampshire, saw “a strange object in the sky” (NAID 28994718, image 39). By the Air Force’s report, taken by telephone, it was a “Continious [sic] band of lights - cigar shaped at all times despite changes of direction”, from which “wings seemed to appear” with red lights on the tips; it stopped and hovered, then seemed “to swoop down in the general direction of their auto”, and as they drove off they heard “a series of short loud ‘buzzes’” (image 40). The record card marks the case “Other”, with “INSUFF DATA” written by hand (our reading), and says the source of the light “is not known” (NAID 28994660, image 1). Four years later the Boston Traveler reported an abduction “related by a New Hampshire couple under clinical hypnosis” (image 30); the file holds that story only in the press.

disclosure-maralinga-1960.title: Maralinga / Wewak
disclosure-maralinga-1960.summary: A formal sighting report filed on the standard RAAF form, working sequentially through meteor, static electricity effects, satellite and “flying saucer” — without resolution.

disclosure-boianai-1959.title: Boianai
disclosure-boianai-1959.summary: On the evening of 26 June 1959 Reverend W. Gill and people of the mission at Boianai watched a bright white light in the north-west, and on it what his data sheet records as “Now three men - moving, glowing, doing something on deck.” That night 38 of them were gathered in one room, three drew what they had seen, and “27 observers of a total of 38 voluntarily signed”. The next evening Gill waved, and “all four now seemed to wave back.” The papers are in a Project Blue Book file: a report of the US Air Attaché in Australia of January 1960, with a civilian society’s report, copies of Gill’s notes and an evaluation by “an interested local agency”, which put at least some of the lights down to the planets Jupiter, Saturn and Mars. The attaché concurred.

disclosure-trindade-1958.title: Trindade Island
disclosure-trindade-1958.summary: A photographer aboard a Brazilian Navy vessel took four photographs of a Saturn-shaped object passing the island. The Navy examined the negatives and the images were released publicly with the endorsement of the President of Brazil — an unusually high-level intervention.

disclosure-levelland-1957.title: Levelland
disclosure-levelland-1957.summary: On the night of 2/3 November 1957 people around Levelland, Texas, reported lights, and some said their vehicles failed. The 1006th Air Intelligence Service Squadron questioned six of them, and its report of 8 November sums up: “Only one observer (Part One) said an object hovered over or on the ground.” Others “saw a light streak across the sky (Parts Three and Four) or a bolt of lightning (Part Five).” (NAID 28972840, image 78) In Part One a student’s engine, lights and radio went out, and when the object left “the motor started with no difficulty” (image 62); in Part Two a barber’s truck engine and lights went out and came back (image 65), an account the reporting officer said “cannot be relied upon” (image 78). The report ends: “this sighting is forwarded as unresolved.” (image 78) The record card concludes “Ball lightning” (image 1).

disclosure-ubatuba-1957.title: The Ubatuba Magnesium
disclosure-ubatuba-1957.summary: On 14 September 1957, by the account of the Aerial Phenomena Research Organization (APRO), a private group in Alamogordo, New Mexico, the columnist Ibrahim Sued of the Rio de Janeiro daily “O Globo” printed a reader’s letter: fishing near Ubatuba, the writer had seen a flying disk explode in flames and had picked up fragments “as light as paper”, a sample of which he enclosed. “The signature was not legible.” The only papers on the event in the Project Blue Book files are a Blue Book list that names it among “NOT CASES”, APRO’s bulletins of 1960, which report analyses in Brazil that found magnesium “of a high degree of purity”, and the correspondence of 1960 in which the Air Force asked APRO for a sample. No laboratory report and no analysis by the Air Force is in the files.

disclosure-rb47-1957.title: RB-47H from Mississippi to Oklahoma
disclosure-rb47-1957.summary: Early on 17 July 1957 an RB-47H electronic reconnaissance aircraft of the 55th Strategic Reconnaissance Wing, callsign Lacy 17, was flying over the southern United States. Near Meridian, Mississippi, its ECM operator No. 2 picked up a signal of “2995 MC TO 3000 MC” that moved up his direction-finding scope, which the wing read as “AN AIRBORNE SOURCE”. From 1010Z the aircraft commander and co-pilot saw a bright light; for the next 90 minutes, as far as Oklahoma City, the wing’s message follows the signal’s bearings and the crew’s sightings, and its intelligence officer had “NO DOUBT” that they coincided. By the same message the air defence site “Utah” confirmed the object on its scopes; the same day the radar squadron at Duncanville, Texas, wrote of “NEGATIVE CONTACT WITH OBJECT”, and the commander called the attempt to find it on the aircraft’s own radar “UNSUCCESSFUL”. Project Blue Book’s record card concludes “Was Aircraft”, with the comment “Identified as american Airlines flight 655.” (NAID 28970538, image 1). The Air Technical Intelligence Center had written: “it is impossible to make any determination from the information submitted. On the other hand, it is difficult to conclude that nothing was present, in the face of the visual and other data presented.” (image 7)

disclosure-lakenheath-1956.title: Bentwaters–Lakenheath
disclosure-lakenheath-1956.summary: On the evening of 13 August 1956 the GCA radar at RAF Bentwaters in England tracked targets that its operators put at up to “more than 4,000 miles per hour”. After midnight the radar centre at RAF Lakenheath tracked targets, ground observers there reported white lights, and an RAF Venom sent after one target reported it on its own radar; Lakenheath’s controllers reported that the target then began “A TAIL CHASE OF THE FRIENDLY FIGHTER”. Project Blue Book’s record card concludes “Anam. [sic] Propagation” (NAID 28966873, image 1), “On the basis of the above, and the limited data provided” (image 3). The same file says the radar and visual sightings “cannot be considered as concurrent” (image 1) and that “From the incomplete information submitted, it is impossible to make a definite determination of the sources of these sightings” (image 33).

disclosure-russell-1955.title: The Train from Baku
disclosure-russell-1955.summary: In October 1955 four Americans on a train from Baku to Tiflis saw lights rise from an airfield between the line and the Caspian Sea. Within six weeks the CIA had written three documents about it: a memorandum after interviewing one of them, a memorandum after interviewing all four, and an unevaluated information report from one of the party. The four described four different things. The CIA found that only one account supported an unconventional aircraft, that the rest could probably be explained as steep-climbing aircraft or missiles, and that the evidence was not firm enough to conclude the Soviets had a radically new type of aircraft.

disclosure-kelly-hopkinsville-1955.title: Kelly–Hopkinsville
disclosure-kelly-hopkinsville-1955.summary: On the night of 21 August 1955 two cars full of people from a farmhouse near Kelly drove to the police station in Hopkinsville and said that little men from a space ship had attacked the house: “We’ve been fighting them for nearly four hours”. They had fired at them with “a shotgun for Sutton and a .22 caliber target pistol for Taylor”. More than a dozen officers went out and found “no tracks of ‘little men’” and no mark of a landing, only a hole in a window screen where the occupants said they had fired. The papers in the US releases are in a Project Blue Book file: a copy of the local paper of 22 August, a statement written that day, a United Press dispatch, and the Air Force’s inquiries of 1956–57. No official investigation is on record; in 1957 the Air Force’s intelligence center wrote that “no credence can be given this almost fantastic report”.

disclosure-newfoundland-1955.title: The KC-97 off Newfoundland
disclosure-newfoundland-1955.summary: On 6 July 1955 the crew of a USAF KC-97 tanker reported an unidentified airborne object in the Newfoundland area, and a ground radar in the same area obtained a return on an object that apparently was the one the crew were watching. A Headquarters USAF intelligence committee could not explain the simultaneous radar returns and visual sightings, tentatively accepted Northeast Air Command's evaluation of an electrical phenomenon and misinterpretation by the crew, classified the incident as an unidentified flying object, and recommended that fighters be scrambled without delay in future incidents of this kind. The crew's accounts, the radar data and the original messages are not in the released file.

washington-1952.title: Washington radar reports
washington-1952.summary: Air traffic controllers and pilots reported unusual radar returns and lights over Washington during July 1952. Historical documents are held in Project Blue Book.

disclosure-tremonton-1952.title: The Tremonton Film
disclosure-tremonton-1952.summary: A Navy warrant officer and professional aerial photographer shot colour film showing a group of bright objects in motion. The material received one of the most detailed analyses in Blue Book history, including densitometric measurement.

disclosure-lubbock-lights-1951.title: The Lubbock Lights
disclosure-lubbock-lights-1951.summary: From the evening of 25 August 1951 professors of Texas Technical College watched formations of lights pass over Lubbock, Texas: “a series of lights in an arcuate formation which covered about 10° in the sky”, in their own report (NAID 28939743, image 84), or “a ‘V’ or ‘U’ shaped set of light-like objects”, in a later summary (image 19). They timed the flights at thirty degrees per second and saw “ten or twevle [sic] flights” up to about 1 November 1951 (image 85). A college freshman photographed formations of lights at the end of August; the papers give the night as both 30 and 31 August. The Air Force’s photographic laboratory wrote: “It is not possible at this time to confirm or deny the authenticity of these negatives as a record of unknown objects against either a starlit or overcast sky.” (image 90) Blue Book’s index files the case as “Other (BIRDS)” (NAID 28921348, image 42).

disclosure-mcminnville-1950.title: The McMinnville Photographs
disclosure-mcminnville-1950.summary: A farming couple took two photographs of a metallic disc-shaped object. The images passed through several independent analyses, including within the Condon Committee, and to this day have no resolution that all researchers accept.

disclosure-oak-ridge-1950.title: Radar over Oak Ridge
disclosure-oak-ridge-1950.summary: Between March 1950 and January 1951 the FBI's file on flying discs collected a run of reports of objects over the Atomic Energy Commission's plant at Oak Ridge, Tennessee. A radio amateur in Knoxville reported an object “directly over Oak Ridge” at up to 100,000 feet on a surplus radar set; the Navy's radar saw nothing, and the Air Force officers who examined his set found it unreliable. In October an Air Force radar at Knoxville tracked eleven objects across the controlled area that a fighter could not find. On 18 December two carloads of officers and engineers saw a bright light over the turnpike, which the three who signed one of the statements compared to sunlight reflected from a distant aircraft. In January 1951 a pilot and the plant's patrol identified a light over the area as a star. The file records every check; none of them found an object, and several of the records it refers to are not in the release.

disclosure-green-fireballs-1948.title: Green Fireballs
disclosure-green-fireballs-1948.summary: A series of vivid green fireballs observed over the most sensitive nuclear installations in the United States. The phenomenon was taken seriously enough that a dedicated observation programme, Project Twinkle, was established with cameras and theodolites.

disclosure-gorman-1948.title: The Gorman Dogfight
disclosure-gorman-1948.summary: Second Lieutenant George Gorman flew an extended series of manoeuvres against a small bright light which, by his account, responded to his movements and out-turned him.

disclosure-chiles-whitted-1948.title: Chiles–Whitted
disclosure-chiles-whitted-1948.summary: Two Eastern Air Lines pilots reported passing a large cigar-shaped object with two rows of bright windows and a flame at the rear. The case was one of the pillars of the internal Project SIGN document said to have argued an interplanetary hypothesis.

disclosure-mantell-1948.title: The Death of Capt. Thomas Mantell
disclosure-mantell-1948.summary: On the afternoon of 7 January 1948 the control tower at Godman Field, Fort Knox, Kentucky, watched an object in the south-western sky after reports of it passed on from the state police. To Lt. Paul I. Orner it “partially appeared as a parachute does with bright sun shining on the top of the silk” (NAID 28930550, image 43); to PFC Stanley Oliver it “had the resemblance of an ice cream cone topped with red” (image 36). The tower asked a flight of four National Guard P-51s passing overhead to try to identify it, and three climbed toward it. By the statement of T/Sgt Quinton A. Blackwell, the flight leader reported it “ahead and above, I'm still climbing” and then: “It appears metallic object of tremendous size” (image 38). The leader was Capt. Thomas F. Mantell (image 40). The last contact was at about 15:15 (image 38), and Mantell’s P-51 “crashed 5 miles SW Franklin, Kentucky” (image 31). The record card has “BALLOON” written by hand (image 1).

roswell-1947.title: Roswell incident
roswell-1947.summary: Reports of recovered debris near Roswell emerged in July 1947. Later US government investigations linked the material to balloon research, and claims of an alien craft were not substantiated.

arnold-1947.title: Kenneth Arnold's pilot report
arnold-1947.summary: On June 24, 1947, pilot Kenneth Arnold described fast-moving objects near Mount Rainier. Early records preserve one of the accounts that brought widespread attention to flying saucers.

disclosure-maury-island-1947.title: The Maury Island Fragments
disclosure-maury-island-1947.summary: In August 1947 the FBI and the Fourth Air Force looked into a story that Harold A. Dahl had seen flying discs near Maury Island, in Puget Sound, and that one of them had showered his boat with debris. The story reached the file second-hand, first in a publisher’s letter of 22 July, and its versions disagree on the date, the number of objects and who was aboard. Two Army Air Forces intelligence officers who heard it in a Tacoma hotel on 31 July, and were handed a box of the supposed fragments, were killed hours later when their B-25 crashed near Kelso; the Army and the FBI found no sabotage. On 7 August Dahl and Fred L. Crisman signed a statement for the FBI calling the material “strange rock formations from a gravel pit on Maury Island”, and an Army Air Forces officer compared it with slag at a smelter. No one who said they had seen the discs ever signed an account of them.

disclosure-ghost-rockets-1946.title: Ghost Rockets
disclosure-ghost-rockets-1946.summary: From late May 1946 the press in Sweden reported flying missiles, which it named “Ghost Rockets”; in June there were reports from Finland and Denmark, by July from Norway, and by the end of July the Swedish Defense Staff had received almost 1,000. The only account from the time in the US releases is a four-page article in the War Department’s Intelligence Review of 9 January 1947. It records descriptions from “a ball of fire with a tail” to a “shiny cigar-shaped object”, no fragments other than “nonmetallic slag”, and Swedish officers who spoke of Soviet rockets but could produce no evidence. Its authors put the high-altitude reports down to meteors or fireworks and thought that a handful of low-flying ones might have been real missiles.

disclosure-foo-fighters-1944.title: Foo Fighters
disclosure-foo-fighters-1944.summary: A file of Air Staff SHAEF in PURSUE release 01 holds 14 extracts from the sortie reports of the 415th Night Fighter Squadron, from ten nights between 14/15 December 1944 and 29/30 January 1945. The crews describe red, orange, yellow, amber, green and white lights, singly, in pairs and in groups, some of which followed their aircraft, one “within 100 ft.” and for “5 minutes”; the squadron called them “Foofighters”. Its intelligence officer wrote: “In every case where pilot called GCI Control and asked if there was a Bogey A/C in the area he received a negative answer.” SHAEF wrote that “it would seem that there must be something more than mere imagination behind the matter”. The Air Ministry suggested Me 262s and flak rockets, and in the same letter: “The whole affair is still something of a mystery”.

disclosure-airship-wave-1896.title: The Airship Wave
disclosure-airship-wave-1896.summary: For six months American newspapers carried thousands of reports of a cigar-shaped “airship” with searchlights and propellers, crossing the country from California eastward. It is the first mass aerial-anomaly wave in the modern record — and it happened before powered flight existed.

disclosure-nuremberg-1561.title: The Nuremberg Phenomenon
disclosure-nuremberg-1561.summary: A broadsheet woodcut describing an “aerial battle” of spheres and crosses above the city. Routinely presented today as evidence of a historical UFO presence — in reality it is a source of an entirely different character from a modern aviation report.
